World.title: UK will 'support Ukraine 100%' despite Russian threat of 'consequences,' PM says
World.content:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the United Kingdom will continue to offer its full and unwavering support to Ukraine despite Russian threats of "consequences."

 

His remarks came after the Russian Embassy in London on Monday warned Westminster would "pay" after UK-made drones were reportedly used in Ukrainian strikes on Russian soil.

The embassy accused the UK of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis" and of "acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator" in Ukrainian attacks.

Responding to the embassy's statement during a trip to Wolverhampton on Tuesday, Burnham said: "This is the UK doing what it has long said it would do, which is to support Ukraine 100% against this illegal war led by Vladimir Putin."

"We are providing support so that Ukraine can defend itself," he continued, adding that the UK was not a "fair-weather" friend and that it would "be there in Ukraine's hour of need."

Ukraine has been ramping up what it calls its "long-range sanctions" on Russia in recent months, launching deep strikes against energy infrastructure and logistics facilities as it seeks to cripple Moscow's economy and grind down Russian President Vladimir Putin's war machine.

Over the weekend, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukrainian forces struck an oil facility in Ust-Luga, close to the Estonian border, as well as Russia's Progress rocket and space centre, a facility involved in the manufacturing and operation of space launch vehicles and rockets, as part of this strategy.

The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine has said that launch vehicles produced at the Progress centre are used to "place Russian military, reconnaissance, and communications spacecraft into orbit."

Russian strikes on Kharkiv kill 10

It comes as Russian missile strikes on a village in the northeastern Ukrainian region of Kharkiv on Tuesday killed at least 10 people and injured 18 others, according to local authorities.

Oleh Syniehubov, the head of the Kharkiv Regional Military Administration, said the attack on Pechenihy also damaged 10 houses and multiple cars and shops.

Russian forces used two Banderol cruise missiles in the strikes, he added.

World.title: Drought reveals Emperor Nero's bridge beneath Rome's Tiber river
World.content:
The remains of an ancient Roman bridge have resurfaced from the Tiber as water levels in Rome fall sharply after weeks without rain.

 

The bridge, traditionally known as Pons Neronis, or Nero's bridge, is located near St Peter's Basilica. Archaeologists say the structure may actually be older than Emperor Nero's reign.

Antonella Bonini, an archaeologist at Rome's cultural heritage superintendence, explains the history of the bridge: “The bridge passes near the villa of Agrippina, the circus of Caligula and then the circus of Nero and traditionally takes the name of Nero, because objectively Nero is the most famous person linked to this area.

"The bridge, however, is considered by scholars to be older (than Nero’s era), built by Caligula, Nero's uncle, to connect the villa of Agrippina, who was Caligula's mother, on the other side, currently roughly corresponding to the Santo Spirito Hospital (near the Vatican) and we assume that it already existed in 39 AD.”

The ruins of the ancient Roman Neronian bridge, emerge from the riverbed of the Tiber river due to drought, in Rome, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. Gregorio Borgia - AP

“We know that it was certainly no longer in use, at least at the end of the third or beginning of the fourth century," said Bonini. "In the registers of ancient Rome’s neighbourhoods (Cataloghi Regionari), which are registers that list the most important monuments of Rome, drawn up between the Diocletian and Constantinian ages, this bridge is no longer mentioned, the Pons Aelius bridge is listed in its place, that is, the bridge that connects Castel Sant'Angelo built by emperor Hadrian to connect his mausoleum with the center of the city.”

The ruins of the ancient Roman Neronian bridge, emerge from the riverbed of the Tiber river due to drought, in Rome, Thursday, Aug. 13, 2026. Gregorio Borgia - AP

Giovanni Giganti, coordinator of Rome Civil Protection centre for water management, says the Tiber is now flowing at well below its historical average: “The Tiber is facing a rather important low-water phase. And this is in fact due to a series of factors including the prolonged drought of these summer months. In fact, the average flow rate in the urban stretch of Rome has fallen below 80 cubic meters per second, against a historical value that is around 150 on average.”

The drought is also part of a wider water crisis affecting Italy. Giganti says the lack of snow in the Apennines has further contributed to the situation:

“We are facing a major water crisis. And it is a crisis that is also due to the fact that this winter we did have quite abundant rainfall, but then the dry periods, as I said before, were quite long and then also another direct cause of this drought is the scarcity of snow on the Apennines.”

As the Tiber continues to run unusually low, the ancient bridge remains visible above the river, offering a rare glimpse of Rome's archaeological past.

World.title: Qatar says it repatriated body of Iranian pilot and denies claims of holding three others
World.content:
Qatar said on Tuesday that an Iranian delegation travelled to Doha and collected the remains of one of its pilots, as Tehran continued to claim that three who went missing after their aircraft entered Qatari airspace and were shot down in March are still in the country.

 

“The body was repatriated, and there was a funeral," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Dr Majed Al Ansari said in Doha, adding that Iran had not responded to Qatar’s invitation to send a technical team to review the search operation.

“We have invited them to send a technical team so that they can review all the details of the search-and-rescue operation,” Al Ansari said.

“Unfortunately, the Iranian side did not respond to this invitation.”

An Iranian military official had earlier accused Qatar of preventing a fact-finding team from entering the country and called on the International Committee of the Red Cross to intervene.

Qatar disputed that account and said its invitation remained open.

“We are here, we are open,” Al Ansari said. “There is no need for media speculation in this case.”

He called Iran’s accusations “false” and “illogical” and suggested they were aimed at an audience inside the country.

“If the agenda is for domestic consumption to solve local issues, we are not concerned in that case,” he said.

Al Ansari's comments came a day after Tehran said it would consider the three missing pilots to be prisoners until Qatar clarified their situation.

Qatar denied holding the pilots in a statement on Saturday, saying it had contacted Iran to coordinate the handover of one pilot’s remains.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said on Monday that Tehran would pursue the case through bilateral, international and legal channels.

What happened to the pilots?

The pilots went missing after Iranian military aircraft entered Qatari airspace on 2 March, during the early days of the war that began with the US-Israeli strikes on Iran on 28 February.

Tehran said the aircraft were taking part in an operation targeting the US Al Udeid Air Base when they were shot down by Qatari forces.

Al Ansari said the aircraft had entered Qatari airspace and threatened people in the country.

“These planes did not come here for leisure,” he said. “They came here to threaten the citizens and residents.”

Qatar tried to contact the pilots but received no response before taking action to defend its territory, he added.

Qatar says its search-and-rescue teams looked for the pilots following the 2 March incident and recovered the remains of one of them. Al Ansari said the search ended on 6 April.

Qatar then contacted Iran to return the remains and invited an Iranian team to review the search details.

“Instead of responding positively to this invitation, we were surprised by these statements,” Al Ansari said.

Qatar says it will defend its territory

Al Ansari further said Doha would continue seeking a diplomatic solution to the ongoing war but would respond firmly to any future attack on the country.

“Iran is not going anywhere, and we are not going anywhere,” he said. “We need to respect the sovereignty of countries, and each side should respect the other.”

“Any attack against our state, we will face it firmly, and we will not hesitate to protect the people, the residents and our land.”

He added that Qatar’s priority remained dialogue and a peaceful end to the crisis.

Al Ansari also said there was no new progress to report in the Iran-Oman talks over reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Qatar was still waiting for the two countries to reach an agreement that could help restore the ceasefire and allow wider US-Iran negotiations to resume, he said.

Asked how close the parties were to reviving the wider US-Iran agreement, Al Ansari said, “I think we are far from this right now.”

He said an agreement to reopen Hormuz would make it easier for wider negotiations to move forward.

World.title: When the city lights up: discovering Uzbekistan after sunset
World.content:
For centuries, Silk Road cities welcomed merchants, pilgrims and travellers. While their landmarks continue to attract visitors during the day, the atmosphere changes noticeably after sunset. As temperatures cool, parks, pedestrian streets and public squares fill with people enjoying the evening outdoors. Restaurants stay open later, cultural venues remain active and families make the most of the cooler hours, particularly during the summer months when daytime temperatures are at their highest.

 

Summer evenings in Samarkand

Samarkand is often associated with monuments such as Registan Square, the Gur-e-Amir Mausoleum and Shah-i-Zinda. After dark, these landmarks remain active as residents and visitors continue walking through the city's historic centre under architectural lighting introduced in recent years. Situated around 740 metres above sea level, Samarkand benefits from cooler evening temperatures during the summer. The combination of fresh air and architectural lighting has gradually made evening visits part of the city's daily routine. Historic monuments remain the main attraction, while nearby parks, cafés and pedestrian areas also become gathering places after work. Local guide Khurshid Narimov says these conditions make evening walks part of everyday life.

“During the day, summer temperatures can be difficult, so people prefer going out in the evening. Families come here to walk, children play around the illuminated monuments, and visitors can continue exploring long after sunset.” Narimov believes lighting has encouraged people to spend more time around historic sites while extending visits beyond daylight hours. He also recommends exploring “Boqiy Shahar” (Eternal City), the Imam al-Bukhari Memorial Complex and traditional craft workshops, many of which remain open in the evening. Australian tourist Jamie Mikic says one of the strongest impressions of Samarkand came from watching local families gather outdoors after dark.

“I love seeing children playing, families walking together and people enjoying the parks. It creates a welcoming atmosphere and gives visitors the opportunity to experience everyday life while exploring the city.”

Bukhara after dark

Several hours west of Samarkand, Bukhara follows a similar rhythm. As the temperature drops, the historic centre becomes busy again with people walking through narrow streets, visiting cafes and gathering around Lyabi-Hauz, Poi Kalyan and the Ark Fortress. According to tour guide Dildora Safarova, the old city takes on a different atmosphere after sunset.

“During the day you see the natural colour of the brick architecture. At night, the monuments are illuminated and the streets become livelier. Musicians perform, dancers invite visitors to join them, and people stay outdoors until late.” Restaurants overlooking the old city have become popular evening destinations. Rooftop terraces offer panoramic views of illuminated monuments, while serving traditional green tea, Uzbek cuisine and contemporary dishes to residents and international visitors. Many venues combine local food with live music and cultural performances that continue into the evening. The compact layout of the old city also allows visitors to explore many of Bukhara's best-known landmarks on foot after dinner. Safarova says evening is also when many artisan workshops, embroidery shops and souvenir stores remain open, giving visitors the opportunity to observe traditional crafts and speak directly with local artisans.

Khiva in evening light

Further west, Khiva offers a different experience. Much of the city's evening life is concentrated within the walls of Ichan-Kala, where monuments, museums and narrow streets are located within a relatively small area. The quieter setting encourages visitors to explore the old city on foot. Tour guide Anaposhsha Boltaeva says many people choose to visit Ichan-Kala in the evening because the weather becomes more pleasant.

“The museums stay open until the evening, and people enjoy walking through Ichan-Kala when it is cooler. Many visitors like photographing the monuments at night because the lighting highlights details that look different from daytime.” She adds that evenings are equally popular with local families, who spend time in nearby parks, recreation areas and the recently developed Arda Khiva complex before returning to the historic centre for a walk.

Evening life in Tashkent

The final stop is Tashkent, where evening activity extends well beyond the historic centre. As Uzbekistan's largest city, the capital offers a broader range of evening activities. Parks, shopping districts, cafés, open-air terraces and pedestrian streets remain busy well into the night, particularly during weekends and the summer. Serbian tour guide Stefan Pavlović says the city's evening atmosphere surprised him.

“Many people don't expect this when they first think about Uzbekistan. After sunset the parks are full, people are walking, meeting friends and enjoying the cooler weather. There is a very relaxed atmosphere.”

Even at 11pm, cafes continue serving customers while families, young people and visitors remain outdoors. Walking has become one of the most popular ways to spend the evening, supported by extensive public spaces and comfortable night-time temperatures. Each destination offers a different evening experience. Samarkand and Khiva invite visitors to explore illuminated historic centres, Bukhara combines architecture with music and dining, while Tashkent's parks and cafés reflect the pace of a modern capital. As temperatures fall, spending time outdoors becomes part of daily life, making the evening one of the busiest times of day for residents and visitors alike.

World.title: Everything you need to know about Meta's biggest legal battle yet
World.content:
A landmark trial against Meta opened on Tuesday in federal court in Oakland, California, in what Kentucky's attorney general has called the largest consumer protection lawsuit in American history.

 

The case could reshape how Facebook and Instagram operate and how social media is experienced more broadly.

Who is suing Meta, and why

The trial is being litigated by four states — California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey — representing a wider coalition of 29 states that first filed the lawsuit in 2023, following a multi-state investigation into Meta's safety practices. The four states were selected to argue the case at trial as a bellwether for the broader coalition.

The states accuse Meta of intentionally designing Facebook and Instagram to be addictive for young users and of concealing what it knew about the resulting harm to their mental health.

"Meta designed Facebook and Instagram to keep kids on the platforms longer and longer — to the point of physical and mental harm. Exploiting our most vulnerable residents to boost corporate profits is not only morally wrong, it's also illegal," said California Attorney General Rob Bonta.

Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman drew a comparison to previous industry-wide legal battles. "AGs are in the perfect position to get this done. We did it with the Tobacco Settlement in the 1990s. We did it with the companies behind the opioid crisis. We'll do it again with Meta," he said.

Meta has denied the allegations. A spokesperson said the states have offered no proof that anyone was misled or harmed and accused them of "chasing an outlandish payout" rather than sticking to the facts.

How much money is at stake

Meta says the states are seeking as much as $1.4 trillion (€1.21tn) in penalties, a figure that would rival the company's market value.

However, the states have told the court that a more realistic damages scenario, if Meta is found liable, would be closer to $200 billion (€173bn).

How the trial will work

The case is being heard by Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers in the US District Court for the Northern District of California.

An eight-person advisory jury has been selected, but the final ruling rests with the judge rather than the jury alone.

The trial is expected to last four to six weeks.

Key witnesses expected to testify include Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram head Adam Mosseri, and Arturo Béjar, a former Meta engineering director turned whistleblower who has testified against the company in previous cases.

What changes are the states demanding

The states want sweeping changes to how Instagram and Facebook operate, including the removal of infinite scroll and public "like" counts.

Infinite scroll, along with other dopamine-driving features, has been linked to severe mental health issues among younger users, including increased anxiety, depression, suicidal thoughts and low self-worth.

Like counts and other engagement metrics have also been linked to young people creating multiple fake accounts to boost engagement with their own posts, which can in turn contribute to depression and a heightened need for social validation.

Other demanded changes include parental verification processes for teenage users, the removal of appearance-altering image filters, an end to video autoplay, and measures to prevent multiple account creation.

The states also want an end to disappearing content such as Instagram Stories, and changes to the recommendation algorithms they accuse of manipulating users' dopamine responses.

These features are core to how Meta keeps users, particularly children and teenagers, engaged for as long as possible.

Constant notifications can make it harder for users to set boundaries around their own usage, even when they want to, while peer pressure and fear of missing out can make it difficult for those who temporarily delete their accounts to stay away.

Meta's track record in court

This is not Meta's first courtroom loss over these claims.

In March, a Los Angeles jury found Meta and Google liable for $6 million (€5.2mn) in damages after a young woman said she became addicted to social media as a child.

Separately, in New Mexico, a jury found in March that Meta had committed 75,000 violations of the state's consumer protection law, resulting in a $375 million (€324mn) penalty.

In August, Judge Bryan Biedscheid ordered a further $567 million (€490mn) penalty in the same case, bringing Meta's total New Mexico exposure to $942 million (€814mn).

That ruling also ordered a series of product changes, including hiding "like" counts by default for under-18s, limiting push notifications to certain hours, imposing monthly usage caps, and barring adults from messaging or being recommended accounts belonging to minors.

Meta has said it will appeal.

World.title: Dressed for power: Giorgia Meloni and the language of fashion
World.content:
From Giorgia Meloni’s shift from dark suits to pastels to Angela Merkel’s signature jackets, politicians have long used clothing to shape how voters see them. In this day and age, power dressing has evolved.

Often dressing in pastel colors, with wide-legged pants falling over her high heels, Italy's first female Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni can't escape fashion scrutiny — and not only because she's the leader of the world's fashion capital.

"Fashion is a language — it tells us what its wearer wants to say without any actual words," Michela Bonafoni, who teaches fashion at Unicollege in Florence, told DW in an interview.



"Perhaps what you wear is very close to your personality. But if you want to give a different impression of yourself, you can also do this through clothing — this is what Meloni does constantly," explained Bonafoni.

Meloni began her tenure as prime minister wearing dark suits as seen in this photo from 2022 Image: IRAQI PRIME MINISTER'S PRESS OFFICE /AFP

Meloni's clothing style can be read as part of a broader political transition: from outsider to establishment figure. When Meloni became prime minister in 2022, her appearance was closely tied to the political identity she had built as a leader of the right-wing Brothers of Italy party with post-fascist roots. Her look: dark suits with chunky boots, serious and even combative.

Enter the concept of "power dressing," which emerged in the 1970s and became influential in the 1980s, as second-wave feminism coincided with more women entering professional and managerial roles. The suit became a way for women to signal authority in traditionally male workplaces. Italian designer Giorgio Armani played a key role — his softer, more fluid tailoring offered a new version of the power suit — borrowing from menswear while creating a more feminine language of authority.

During her first official public appearances, Meloni was often seen in dark Armani suits, a nod to traditional power dressing, and a look that said, according to Bonafoni: "I'm here in this kind of government and that's all there is to it."

From masculine suits to pastels

Since then, Meloni's look has softened — she's often seen in wide-legged silhouettes and suits in cream, beige, pink and other muted or pastel shades. The style change also coincides with how she has become a more established figure in European politics, moving closer to the European Union and becoming a prominent supporter of Ukraine. Yet, Meloni has maintained a conservative approach to domestic politics, which hasn't gone down well with much of the public — including many in the country's fashion industry. No luxury brand, including Armani, publicly stepped forward to style her or support her use of their clothing.

This hasn't stopped Meloni from using fashion to appeal to a broader public. "When Meloni understood that many Italians didn't like some of the actions of her government, she started to wear the pastel colors, which incite understanding and say 'I'm Giorgia, a woman who is kind,'" said Bonafoni. The author also points out that Meloni sports "Made in Italy" designers as part of her brand of nationalism — attaching its power to her own.

Meloni often wears wide trousers and softer colors Image: Chris Emil Janßen/picture alliance

At the Salone del Mobile, Italy's premier design event in Milan this past April, Meloni chose a casual look: jeans and a casual beige blazer. "Her look said: I'm casual because I'm just like you — but I'm also exactly where I want to be right now in this moment and in this government," said Bonafoni. Such a style exudes confidence and is closer to the more relaxed style of female politicians in the US, Bonafoni added.

Merkel wore a distinctive 'uniform' during the years she served as Germany's chancellor Image: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

A political 'uniform'

But political power doesn't always require a changing wardrobe. For some women leaders, consistency itself can become a form of power dressing.

Former German Chancellor Angela Merkel developed one of the most recognizable wardrobes in modern politics. Her formula was remarkably consistent: trousers and a three-button jacket, with the jackets appearing in an extraordinary range of colors. The simplicity itself became a kind of uniform, putting Merkel herself, as a politician, rather than her fashion, at the center. "Her 'second skin' of clothing was very close to her character, her attitudes and political decisions she made," points out Bonafoni.



Former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher also had her fashion 'uniforms' so to speak, down pat. Her appearance was carefully constructed — tailored suits, pearls, handbags — an instantly recognizable version of feminine political authority in her era.

These days, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum offers another prime example of a politician who wears clothing to send a message. She frequently wears garments made by women artisans from Mexico to show her support and solidarity with Mexico's Indigenous communities.

Mexican President Claudia Scheinbaum is known for wearing clothing made by women in indigenous communities Image: Carlos Santiago/Eyepix Group/IMAGO

From hipster dad to tactical wear

While the few women politicians we have on the world stage fall under increased fashion scrutiny, men too have long understood the political power of appearance — perhaps now more than ever. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy often chooses to wear tactical clothing that's far from the standard suit and tie look of most world leaders.

As Ukrainian journalist Illia Ponomarenko told Politico in an interview last year, it's part of his anti-elitist message, one that directly confronts the world leaders he meets. "His clothes are basically asking: What are you about? Are you about the business of saving lives, or are you about fancy protocols?" said Ponomarenko. "Even when he meets with kings, he dresses in a way that represents the average Ukrainian involved in this war effort. It's a message to say, 'I've come to the corners of power as a representative of my humble people.'"



Similarly, the UK's Labour Party Prime Minister Andy Burnham, whose look has been referred to as "hipster dad," chooses smart-casual styles; T-shirts, polo shirts and trainers. It's a political messaging move that says he's on the same level as the public.



As for Giorgia Meloni, Bonafoni expects the world will soon see another style change as she is challenged by far-right politician and former army general Roberto Vannacci. "Meloni has said she doesn't want Vannacci in her government, but her party will need him in a coalition if it wants to remain in power," says Bonafoni. "I'm sure if and when Vannacci challenges her, she will change her style again because she'll have to present herself as someone who's even more powerful."



This article was edited by Tenzin Sekhon

World.title: Syria, US condemn Israeli strikes on military base
World.content:
Israel has not officially claimed the strikes on Abu al-Duhur airbase in Idlib, some 70 kilometers from the Turkish border. US envoy Tom Barrack called the Israeli strikes an "unnecessary escalation."

Eight Israeli airstrikes hit an unused airbase in northwestern Syria's Idlib province early on Tuesday, Syrian state media reported, in attacks widely condemned by Damascus and Washington.

The attacks struck the runway and storage facilities at Abu al-Duhur base, Syrian state-run broadcaster Al-Ikhbariya reported, some 70 kilometers (43.5 miles) from the Turkish border.

Turkey is a key ally of Syria's interim government, in power since ousting former President Bashar Assad in a December 2024 lightning offensive.

What else do we know about the Israeli airstrikes on the Idlib airbase?

Syrian state media, quoting a military source, said that "Israeli occupation aircraft early this morning targeted the runway" of the base "with eight strikes," damaging infrastructure but without causing casualties.

The facility has been out of service as a dedicated military base for over a decade. The Reuters news agency cited an unnamed military source as saying it has been used as a training center for Syria's new army since Assad's 2024 ouster.

Israel has yet to officially comment on the attacks.

They come on the heels of a Turkish military delegation's visit to the airfield, according to the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights monitor. According to the UK-based monitor, the visit was part of efforts to reactivate the base.

The strikes caused damage but Syrian media reported they left no casualties Image: REUTERS

How did the US, Syria react to the attacks?

Tom Barrack, US ambassador to Turkey and special presidential envoy for Syria and Iraq, condemned the Israeli strikes in a post on X.

"We are deeply concerned that the confirmed Israeli airstrikes on Abu al-Duhur Airbase constitute an unnecessary escalation that does not advance regional stability," Barrack wrote.

He defended Syria's interim administration of Ahmed al-Sharaa, who once led an Al-Qaeda-affiliated militant group but has since distanced himself from Islamist militancy. Barrack stressed Sharaa's administration "repeatedly indicated a preference for de-escalation with Israel."

"We encourage all parties to prioritize logical discourse over further military incidents," he said.

Netanyahu's endless wars: How dangerous are they for Israel? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Syria's Foreign Ministry also condemned the strikes, calling them "an unjustified act of aggression."

It urged the international community and the United Nations Security Council to "take a firm position against Israel's repeated violations of Syrian sovereignty."

The "continuation of these Israeli attacks" since December 2024 came while Syria "has exercised restraint and worked to consolidate stability and avoid escalation," it added.

Tense Israeli-Turkish relations overshadowed by Syria

Since Assad's ouster, Israel has launched hundreds of strikes on Syria, sending troops to a United Nations-patrolled buffer zone that had separated Israeli and Syrian forces in Syria's Israeli-occupied Golan since 1974.

How Golan Heights Druze community views post-Assad Syria To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The Israeli army has also carried out regular incursions deeper inside Syrian territory.

Israeli officials have declared their intention to keep forces in a self-declared "security zone" in southern Syria.

Turkey has accused Israel of trying to destabilize Syria and its new administration, which Ankara has been helping by training its army and assisting with building its state institutions and infrastructure.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz has directly warned Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan, stressing Israel would now allow steps that strengthen Syria's military capabilities in ways that could threaten Israel.

Edited by: Saim Dušan Inayatullah

World.title: Should India be worried about the Mecca defense pact?
World.content:
A defense agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkey brings Islamabad deeper into the security architecture of the Middle East. How is India planning to respond?

The "Mecca Joint Defense Agreement" signed by Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan on August 7, comes amid the Iran war and shifting security arrangements in the Middle East.

Saudi Arabia is seeking additional security partnerships amid uncertainty over the reliability of the US security umbrella. Turkey is seeking a larger regional role, while Pakistan is looking to turn its longstanding military relationship with Riyadh into wider strategic influence.

The agreement calls for collective defense, stating an armed attack on one member will be regarded as an attack on all three.

It also formalizes relationships that already exist. Pakistan has trained and assisted Saudi forces for decades, while its defense relationship with Turkey has expanded through military exchanges and cooperation.

For India, the question is whether the pact gives arch-rival Pakistan a deeper role in a region central to Indian interests.

Pact changes little on the ground for India

Some Indian analysts see little immediate change in the regional balance. Others see a warning that India needs a stronger security presence in a region where its economic interests have grown considerably.

India has ramped up defense spending in recent years Image: Adnan Abidi/REUTERS

Saudi Arabia is a major energy and investment partner for New Delhi. The Gulf and the Red Sea are vital to India's trade and energy security.

The pact allows Pakistan to expand on its security role in the Gulf while providing an institutional framework for closer defense cooperation and potentially greater access to funding and technology.

However, former Indian High Commissioner to Pakistan Ajay Bisaria believes the agreement will have little effect on the basic dynamics of an India Pakistan confrontation.

"The Mecca Pact is not worth the paper it's written on," Bisaria told DW.

"It does little to move the needle beyond the Saudi-Pakistan defense pact of last year, an arrangement that proved to have only signaling value for Iran, the US and Israel, at a moment when Riyadh was unsettled by the frailty of the American security umbrella," he added.

In the event of a future India Pakistan crisis, the former ambassador said he does not expect the pact to fundamentally alter Saudi Arabia's position.

"For India, this is a pact to be monitored, not one to be unduly concerned about," Bisaria said.

"In the event of another terrorist attack from Pakistan, the situation is unlikely to look very different from Operation Sindoor, save, perhaps, for some added rhetoric," he said, referring to the name of India's response to a 2025 attack on tourists in Kashmir that New Delhi blames on Pakistan-backed militants. Islamabad denies any involvement in the attack.

"Turkey would continue to supply drones and equipment to Pakistan, while the Saudis, far from rushing to position themselves as its defenders, are more likely to offer their services, more vocally, as mediators," he said.

No immediate concern for India

Tara Kartha, former member of the National Security Council Secretariat, believes India should not overstate the significance of the agreement.

"India doesn't need to be overly concerned about the Mecca pact. Saudi Arabia and Turkey hardly see us as a strategic competitor or an 'enemy'," Kartha told DW.

Much of the Pakistan-Turkey military relationship already exists, Kartha added. "Turkey's formidable defense industry will certainly be made available for the pact's constituents,” she said.

"But Pakistan and Turkey already have a strong defense relationship including joint development of the Kaan aircraft. So, nothing really changes on the ground barring possibly increased funding for the Pakistan defense budget. That is certainly a problem that can't be easily circumvented," added Kartha.

The more immediate concern for India may be whether Saudi resources and Turkish technology could strengthen Pakistan's military capabilities over time.

India's ties with Saudi Arabia

Beyond the India-Pakistan rivalry, the pact also raises questions about India's ties with Saudi Arabia.

The kingdom has built a substantial relationship with India, spanning energy, investment, trade and political ties. And Riyadh's effort to diversify its security partnerships does not necessarily mean choosing Pakistan over India.

Geopolitical analyst Harsh Pant, vice president at the Delhi-based Observer Research Foundation (ORF), told DW that India should respond cautiously but not passively.

"The different strategic interests of the three members could limit the pact's cohesion, but New Delhi should use its own relationship with Riyadh to deepen security, intelligence and economic cooperation," Pant said.

Deeper bilateral ties with Saudi Arabia, he added, could help ensure that Pakistan's new role does not translate into disproportionate influence in the Gulf.

New Delhi will also have to watch the military dimension closely. If Turkish drones, missiles, electronic warfare systems or other defense technologies become more readily available to Pakistan, India's western security calculations could change.

What's behind Pakistan's deepening ties with Saudi Arabia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

A wake-up call for India?

Randhir Jaiswal, spokesperson for India's Ministry of External Affairs, said that New Delhi was examining the pact's implications "from the perspective of India's national security and considerations of regional peace and stability."

"India remains fully committed to safeguarding its national interests and will take all necessary measures in this regard," he said.

Strategic expert C. Raja Mohan told DW that the trilateral agreement points to a larger problem in India's approach to the Gulf. India's economic dependence on the region has grown considerably, while its security presence has remained comparatively limited, he said.

"For India, this should be a warning that New Delhi cannot remain primarily a diplomatic and economic player in the Gulf. It needs greater military reach in the region and deeper, practical security and defense relationships with individual Middle Eastern countries," Mohan said.

He sees a widening mismatch between India's interests and its security presence.

"The gap between India's economic interests and its limited military-security presence is becoming harder to ignore," he added.

India could deepen defense and intelligence cooperation with Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states, strengthen maritime security in the Arabian Sea and Red Sea, and closely monitor Pakistan-Turkey military cooperation.

Mohan, a professor of American Studies at Jindal Global University, sees the agreement principally as an attempt by Saudi Arabia to widen its options.

"I see it more as evidence of the Arab states' continuing inability to build a dependable regional security system and, importantly, as Saudi Arabia hedging against uncertainty over the reliability of the US security umbrella," Mohan said.

Edited by: Wesley Rahn

World.title: Fact check: How do I spot AI-generated images?
World.content:
Images created or manipulated with artificial intelligence tools are flooding social media. How can you know what’s real and what’s not? Here are a few tips.

Anyone with an internet connection and access to an artificial intelligence (AI) tool can create photorealistic images within seconds, for free or for very little money, and then spread them on social networks at breakneck speed.

The tools used to create AI-generated images are improving rapidly, reducing the number of obvious AI errors – often referred to as AI hallucinations – and making it increasingly difficult for users to determine whether a viral image depicts a real event.

Gone are the days when AI tools routinely produced images of public figures with four fingers, an excessive amount of teeth or unnatural body proportions.

An additional challenge is that while many images are entirely AI-generated, others are real photos that have been partially altered using AI.

This AI-manipulated image of a Hitler look-alike allegedly attending a 2026 World Cup match garnered millions of views on social media Image: X

Here’s one example: an authentic broadcast image from the 2026 World Cup in which a fan was replaced by an Adolf Hitler lookalike.

Of course, the image was actually created using an OpenAI-powered tool.

So how can you spot AI-generated images? DW Fact check offers tips to help you navigate today's information landscape.

Look closely at the picture

There a several tell-tale signs that give away that this image was generated with the help of AI, most notably gibberish-filled text Image: X

You may remember the story of a Syrian teenager who helped stop a knife attack in the German city of Hamburg in 2025.

As the story spread, conflicting accounts of the incident emerged on social media, along with AI-generated images like the one above.

The image looks authentic at first glance, but if you zoom in and examine it carefully, you’ll find obvious inconsistencies.

That's why it's important to take your time and inspect the details. Common AI errors might be hidden in the background, including distorted objects and gibberish-filled text.

Putin is supposed to have knelt down in front of Xi Jinping, but a closer looks shows that the picture is fake Image: Twitter/DW

If your device doesn't allow you to zoom in far enough, online tools can help.

A tool we often use at DW Fact check is Forensically , a free online photo forensics platform that includes a magnifier and other features for examining images closely.

Think about the context

Remember the Hitler lookalike from above? A supporter resembling the Nazi dictator would almost certainly have attracted immediate attention from broadcasters, stadium officials and other spectators.

Fact check: How do I spot AI images? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Yet no reputable media organizations reported such a stir, and no fans in the stadium shared posts showing the lookalike from a different perspective.

This example highlights a key verification technique: move beyond the pixels and ask yourself whether the event itself makes sense.

One way of doing that is checking whether the apparent event has been covered by trustworthy news organizations.

If an image appears to show a highly unusual or controversial incident, but there is no evidence of it in credible reporting, that should raise a red flag.

You can also look at who’s posting and sharing the image. If the account often shares AI-generated material or appears to have no connection to the event itself, it’s wise to treat the image with caution.

Find the image source

If you're unsure whether an image is real or generated by AI, try to find its source.

One way to do this is by conducting a so-called reverse image search. Instead of searching with keywords, you can upload an image to tools like Google Images or TinEye .

These tools can help answer several questions:

When was the image first uploaded?

On which platforms is the image being shared?

What are users saying about it in comments and posts?

Have any reputable fact-checkers already verified the image?

Of course, some AI-generated images may be brand new and therefore produce few or no results.

But manipulated images are often based on older, authentic pictures. In those cases, a reverse search can reveal the original image and provide important context.

If you find that an image has already been fact-checked, one way to assess the credibility of the article or video is to see whether the organization is certified by the International Fact Checking Network (IFCN) .

The IFCN assesses fact-checkers against a set of professional standards, which include being as fair and transparent as possible, being non-partisan, and committing to open and honest corrections.

You can find a list of IFCN-certified outlets here , including DW Fact check.

The IFCN should not be confused with the Global Fact-Checking Network (GFCN), a Russian platform with close ties to the Kremlin.

Use AI tools with caution

AI detectors can help assess whether an image was created or modified using AI. They search for invisible watermarks and other digital traces associated with AI-generated content.

There are a few different types.

Tech companies such as Google and OpenAI, the creator of ChatGPT, have developed systems that identify whether their own AI models were used to create or modify an image.

Google's SynthID tool can be accessed here , and here is the link to OpenAI's verification tool.

A search using OpenAI, the US-based organization behind ChatGPT, indicates that its tools were used to create the image of the Hitler lookalike Image: Open AI

Other tools, such as Image Whisperer , AI or Not , and Hive Moderation, estimate the likelihood that an image was manipulated using AI.

And then AI chatbots, such as X’s Grok, can provide answers to user questions on whether images are real or fake.

In the Hitler lookalike example, OpenAI identified a digital watermark, which confirmed it was manipulated using the AI company’s tools.

One important word of caution: AI detectors often make mistakes.

Their findings should not be treated as definitive proof, but rather as one piece of the verification puzzle.

If possible, use more than one tool and cross-check the results to reduce the risk of drawing the wrong conclusions.

A viral image of a young girl begging for food in Gaza was wrongly identified by Grok as a photo from Iraq taken in 2014. Image: X

When in doubt, don’t share

Even after following all these steps, you may still be unsure whether an image is real or AI generated.

As AI technology continues to improve, distinguishing between authentic and AI-generated images is becoming increasingly difficult.

If you cannot verify an image with confidence, our recommendation is simple: don’t share it, especially on social media.

Instead, consider warning friends and family members privately that the image’s authenticity has not been confirmed and that it should be treated with caution.

And if you’re still unsure, you can always send the image to us at factchecking@dw.com. We may be able to help verify its authenticity.

This article was first published in 2023 and has been revised to incorporate new developments and trends. Joscha Weber and Kathrin Wesolowski contributed to that report. Edited by Josh Axelrod.

World.title: Designing food for a hotter world
World.content:
Inside futuristic labs, plants are scanned, stressed and analysed. The aim is to use the results to produce plant strains that can better serve a growing population in a warming world.

Rows of tomato saplings stand in a room packed with cameras. Just a few weeks old, they're under constant surveillance as scientists monitor them for tiny changes in color, temperature and photosynthesis.

These plants are growing in a chamber designed to mimic the heat and humidity of India's climate. By analyzing their reactions to different stressors, researchers at Wageningen University in the Netherlands are aiming to uncover genetic traits that have the potential to make crops resilient to human-caused climate change.

"We can regulate the temperature. We can give them a heat stress phase, we can freeze shortly, so we can simulate night frost, which could be very disruptive for young plants," explains Rick van de Zedde, program manager at the Netherlands Plant Eco-phenotyping Centre (NPEC). "We can introduce salinity by adding salt."

In fact, the scientists can simulate almost any condition on the planet. "I would call it a gym for plants," van de Zedde adds.

Why understanding plants is so important

It's research that's becoming ever more essential. Agriculture has traditionally relied on predictable seasons and conditions, with farmers planning around established weather patterns, planting in the spring and harvesting in the autumn, for example.



But as societies burn fossil fuels that heat the planet, rising global temperatures are disrupting that rhythm.

Farmers are grappling with more unpredictable weather conditions as a result of a warming world Image: Fethi Belaid/AFP/Getty Images

Increasing heatwaves, longer and more intensive droughts, as well as severe flooding caused by global heating is increasingly putting crops at risk.

Following soaring temperatures this summer, farmers in some regions of Germany are warning of harvest failure. Grain production losses have already been registered in countries including France, Hungary and the United Kingdom.

With the global population predicted to hit 10 billion by 2050, the pressure is on to produce enough food. That race is intensified by rising meat consumption, which implies growing more grain for animal feed.

Simultaneously, demand for crops to use as biofuels, which are made from organic material including plants or animal waste, is also on the rise.

So for researchers, the question is no longer just how to grow more food, but how to do so under increasingly challenging conditions.

A high-tech way ahead

Dubbed the 'Silicon Valley' of agriculture, the Netherlands has long been a leader in farming innovation. Despite its relatively small size, the country is the world's second largest exporter for agricultural products by value — after the US.

Researchers say crossbreeding plant varieties could help them grow with traits more resilient to a hotter climate Image: Manuel Vering/DW

Inside the Wageningen University greenhouses, scientists recreate environmental conditions such as drought, tropical humidity or frosty nights, and use a range of technology to monitor the plants.

Over a period of weeks, automated scales record the weights of tree species every three minutes to reveal how much water they need. And sophisticated scanners track the movement of leaves as part of a process known as phenotyping — which measures plants and their features.



Though botanists have been tracking flora for thousands of years to select the best plants, the processes were historically manual and therefore slow and painstaking.

"All the lab measurements were restricting the size of the experiments," van de Zedde tells DW. "If you look around here in NPEC, you see that we are talking about thousands of plants in one experiment."

Taking experiments into the field

Despite the sophistication of the lab, it cannot completely mirror real-world conditions. Factors like hail storms, high winds or differing soil temperatures, remain difficult to recreate.

Near the university, experimental barley fields provide an important reality check. It is there that researchers deploy mobile imaging and use GPS positioning systems to collect data on hundreds of crop varieties in the field.

By comparing greenhouse and field results, they are better able to identify the plant traits that will be help produce food that is going to be resilient to a changing climate.

"It's all about fitness. We simply score: how do these plants respond to the stress? Which ones can cope with it, which ones suffer from it," says van de Zedde.

Scientists are able to test thousands of plants in closely monitored greenhouses Image: Manuel Vering/DW

Researchers can use the data to see the DNA profiles linked to tolerance to certain stressors. They can then cross breed varieties — one with a high yield and one that is robust, for example, to produce resilient offspring.

What's next for the research?

The goal is to fast forward evolution. The Netherlands government and plant-breeding companies funding the research, will decide which variants to continue to breed.

But Alan Pauls, PhD candidate in the university's Laboratory of Genetics says the process has been met with criticism from some quarters.

"When you talk to the older generation, I definitely do feel like they don't trust it," he says. "The moment you talk about taking food or plants into a lab, immediately who you think about is GMO."

Why does genetic engineering have such a bad image? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Genetically modified organisms, or GMOs, have had their genes changed artificially to make them take on a particular characteristic. One way it's done is to insert a gene from a different species, like bacteria, into a plant.

In the European Union, genetic modification is strictly legally regulated and requires rigorous safety checks. At Wageningen, just 5% of experiments involve genetically modified plants. Most focus on selecting existing traits through phenotyping, speeding up natural processes rather than creating new characteristics.

Pauls believes the argument that too much interference makes food artificial is outdated.

"Are we thinking that it's artificial because a machine is involved? Are we thinking that it's artificial because it's happening so fast, or it's happening in a lab?" he says. "I can still harvest rice with a sickle, but is it going to feed a billion people in time? No."

Edited by: Tamsin Walker



This article was adapted from a video from DW's Planet A series.

World.title: German court convicts Ukrainian man over Russia parcel plot
World.content:
The court said the man sent packages with GPS trackers from Germany to Ukraine to scope out potential sabotage targets for Russian secret services.

A German court has sentenced a 30-year-old Ukrainian man to one year and three months in prison over a Russian plot to carry out acts of sabotage.

Two other Ukrainian men, aged 22 and 25, were acquitted.

The higher regional court in the city of Stuttgart said the three were involved in sending packages with GPS trackers from Germany to Ukraine using a Ukrainian parcel service.

According to prosecutors, the aim was to reveal the precise transport routes and pass the information on to Russian secret services.

In a second step, prosecutors said the men were planning to dispatch packages designed "to ignite in Germany or elsewhere en route to parts of Ukraine not occupied by Russia and cause as much damage as possible in order to undermine the population's sense of security."

However, the plan was discovered before it could be implemented.

Acts of sabotage linked to Russia surge in Europe To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Spying for the purpose of sabotage

The three men were arrested in May last year.

The 30-year-old who was given jail time "intentionally participated in scouting potential sabotage targets for a Russian state entity," the court said.

He was found guilty of "spying for the purposes of sabotage."

The court said he involved the other two defendants in the shipment of GPS trackers. However, it could not be proven that those two suspects knew their actions were part of a sabotage plot.

The prosecution called for sentences ranging from two years and nine months to four years and three months, while the defense argued for acquittal for all three defendants.

Both ​the convicted defendant and the prosecutors have the right to appeal.

The enemy within: Ukrainian teenagers recruited by Russia To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Why might Germany be a target?

Germany is Ukraine's most important supporter in the war with Russia and has been on high alert for suspected sabotage and spying operations coordinated by Moscow.

In a previous case, a series of exploding parcels were shipped from Lithuania in 2024 and detonated in Germany, Poland and Britain. Security sources blamed Russia, although Moscow has denied involvement in such operations.

An explosives-laden drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport earlier in August Image: Sebastian Willnow/dpa/picture alliance

Earlier this month, a drone equipped with explosives and a detonator was discovered near a Ukrainian cargo aircraft at eastern Germany's Leipzig Airport, a key military equipment hub.

German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt described it as a "hybrid" attack by a "foreign power" but did not name Russia. Moscow has dismissed suggestions that it was responsible.

World.title: Belgium wildfire: Rains help High Fens containment efforts
World.content:
Firefighters continue to battle one of the worst wildfires in Belgian history near the German border. Rains and cooler temperatures are helping them bring it to heel after it ravaged an area half the size of Manhattan.

Belgian firefighters were pushing to encircle and contain the country's largest wildfire in a century.

Rain and cooler temperatures provided some natural relief against the blaze on Tuesday but also teamed up with winds to hamper air support and waterbombing operations.

The fire expanded to cover an area of around 3,000 hectares — about half the size of Manhattan in New York — by Monday.

The High Fens, or Hautes Fagnes, nature reserve is a vast expanse of boggy peatlands, pine forests and hiking trails, with parts of it difficult to access with large machinery, except from above.

Light rain fell on Tuesday morning, with heavier precipitation forecast later — this both helped to douse the fire naturally but also hampered efforts to use planes and helicopters to drop water en masse from above Image: Sascha Thelen/dpa/picture alliance

What's the latest on the firefighting efforts?

"We are trying to definitively encircle the fire today," regional government spokesman Niolas Yernaux told the AFP news agency on Tuesday.

Firefighters worked through the night to try to make a crucial link-up between the eastern and northern fronts, despite difficult access conditions in the hilly and wooded area.

The hilly and densely forested nature reserve is dotted with rough farm tracks and hiking trails, not an abundance of paved roads suited to heavy machinery Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

"We're talking about one or two kilometers, and we're on the verge of achieving it," Yernaux said.

He said that the fire was "under control and contained" in areas where firefighters could operate.

Belgium's interior minister warned the fire was so vast that efforts to douse it and prevent it from rekindling would need to be thorough and could take weeks, even once it is extinguished Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

However, Yernaux said the hard-to-reach front stretching towards the German border and the town of Monschau remained a concern; much of this area is only really accessible from above. The wind and rain could delay such aerial operations, potentially until Tuesday evening, he warned.

How far from the border is the fire, what's the situation in Monschau?

Residents of Monschau have already been told to leave their homes because of the smoke hazard, with the fire roughly 2.3 kilometers (roughly 1.5 miles) from the border. Yernaux said that "strong winds" were blowing towards the east and the German frontier.

Firefighters and civilian emergency response crews are on hand in Monschau, some of them also assisting colleagues in Belgium Image: Oliver Berg/dpa/picture alliance

"At the moment it's manageable," Monschau fire service spokesman Tobias Schnell told the dpa news agency. Should the winds pick up further, he said that could fan the flames in the town's direction.

He said that water tanks and other equipment had already been placed in its potential path in case it is needed. He said around 170 people were working on a three-shift rotation around the clock, and that authorities were working on the assumption the operation would last several more days at least.

Flames could be seen from the border overnight at the peak of the blaze Image: Thomas Banneyer/dpa/picture alliance

Smoke has spread dozens of kilometers to the east, with major cities like Cologne and Wuppertal both warning residents of the risk of poor air quality and smoke.

"At present the smell of the fire can be perceived throughout the city," Wuppertal's fire department warned, recommending that people close doors and windows. "A health risk cannot be ruled out."

Locals start to return, but still urged to limit movements

Villagers in places like Sourbrodt, which was evacuated at the peak of the fire over the weekend, started returning to their homes as the threat subsided on Monday evening.

Nevertheless, the local Waimes municipality asked residents to exercise continued caution.

"Residents are asked to limit travel within this area to what is strictly necessary and to act with particular vigilance and responsibility," it said. "Despite the return of evacuated residents, operations carried out by the various emergency, security and response services remain a priority and must be able to proceed under the best possible conditions."

Affected areas of the nature reserve itself are also strictly off limits for summer hikers at present Image: Yves Herman/REUTERS

Two villages in the Bütgenbach municipality, meanwhile, remain cleared, with conditions not yet safe there.

Wallonia's Agriculture Ministry also said on Tuesday that it would review compensation for farmers who volunteered to help with the firefighting efforts.

Farmers in the area turned their machinery into water transporters or helped to try to clear foliage from the path of the fire to halt or slow its spread Image: Nicolas Lambert/Belga/dpa/picture alliance

This is was "under review — regarding both the substance and the procedure, as well as the legal feasiblity of doing so," Agriculture Minister Anne-Catherine Dalcq's office said on Tuesday.

This followed an appeal from the presdient of the Royal Federation of Belgian Firefighters, who demanded reciprocal aid after the farmers' help battling the blaze.

"Who will cover the cost of the equipment damaged during this operation? Without them, the situation would be far worse," Marc Gilbert had said in an interview with the Belga news agency.

European aircraft join battle as Belgium's wildfire spreads To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The vast fire gathered pace just after another a few kilometers east across the German border in the Hürtgenwald forest was contained late last week.
